questions.question: Which type of health check is ALWAYS enabled in an Auto Scaling Group and cannot be disabled?

options.text: ELB health checks
EC2 health checks
Custom health checks
CloudWatch health checks

explanation.correct: EC2 health checks are always enabled in every Auto Scaling Group and monitor the system-level status of instances.
explanation.why: ELB health checks are optional (but recommended). CloudWatch and Custom are not a default ASG health check type.

questions.question: What does an ELB health check do that an EC2 health check cannot?

options.text: Detects hardware failures on the physical host
Checks the application's HTTP response on a configured endpoint
Monitors CPU utilization thresholds
Verifies IAM role permissions on the instance

explanation.correct: ELB health checks probe a configured URL path (like /health) and check for a valid HTTP response — detecting app-level failures.
explanation.why: Hardware failure detection is EC2's job. CPU monitoring is CloudWatch. IAM is unrelated to health checks.

questions.question: What is the default health check grace period in an Auto Scaling Group?

options.text: 60 seconds
120 seconds
300 seconds
600 seconds

explanation.correct: The default health check grace period is 300 seconds (5 minutes), giving new instances time to finish booting before health checks begin.
explanation.why: 60 and 120 are too short for most applications. 600 is not the default though it can be configured.

questions.question: Which scaling policy adds a FIXED number of instances regardless of how far the metric has exceeded the threshold?

options.text: Target Tracking Scaling
Step Scaling
Simple Scaling
Predictive Scaling

explanation.correct: Simple Scaling adds a fixed number of instances (e.g., always +2) when the CloudWatch alarm fires, no matter how severe the breach is.
explanation.why: Step Scaling varies based on severity. Target Tracking manages its own instance count. Predictive uses ML forecasting.

questions.question: Which CloudWatch alarm state triggers an Auto Scaling action?

options.text: OK
ALARM
INSUFFICIENT_DATA
PENDING

explanation.correct: The ALARM state is when the metric has breached the defined threshold — this is what triggers scaling actions.
explanation.why: OK means the metric is within bounds. INSUFFICIENT_DATA means not enough data yet. PENDING is an ASG instance state, not a CloudWatch alarm state.

questions.question: What happens during the cooldown period in Simple Scaling?

options.text: The ASG doubles the number of instances
All health checks are paused
No further scaling actions occur even if the alarm is still firing
The Load Balancer stops routing traffic

explanation.correct: During the cooldown period, ASG ignores additional alarm firings — no further scaling in or out occurs until the cooldown expires.
explanation.why: Doubling instances is not what happens. Health checks continue during cooldown. Load Balancer is unaffected.

questions.question: Which scaling policy allows you to define DIFFERENT instance additions based on how badly a threshold is exceeded?

options.text: Simple Scaling
Scheduled Scaling
Step Scaling
Predictive Scaling

explanation.correct: Step Scaling uses step adjustments — for example, add 1 instance at 60-70% CPU, add 2 at 70-85%, add 4 above 85%. The response matches the severity.
explanation.why: Simple Scaling always adds the same fixed number. Scheduled is time-based. Predictive uses ML forecasting.

questions.question: What does Step Scaling use instead of a cooldown period?

options.text: Grace period
Instance warmup
Deregistration delay
Alarm evaluation period

explanation.correct: Step Scaling uses an instance warmup period — the time given for a newly launched instance to contribute to metric data before another scaling action is evaluated.
explanation.why: Grace period is for health checks. Deregistration delay is for Load Balancer connection draining. Alarm evaluation period is a CloudWatch concept.

questions.question: Which scaling policy uses machine learning to forecast demand and provision instances BEFORE the spike arrives?

options.text: Step Scaling
Scheduled Scaling
Target Tracking Scaling
Predictive Scaling

explanation.correct: Predictive Scaling analyzes historical traffic data using ML and proactively launches instances before expected demand — so you're never playing catch-up.
explanation.why: Step Scaling reacts to current alarms. Scheduled is for known time patterns. Target Tracking maintains a target value reactively.

questions.question: You want to keep CPU utilization automatically around 50% without defining specific scaling amounts. Which policy is best?

options.text: Simple Scaling
Step Scaling
Target Tracking Scaling
Scheduled Scaling

explanation.correct: Target Tracking lets you define a target metric value (e.g., 50% CPU) and AWS automatically adjusts the instance count to maintain that target.
explanation.why: Simple and Step Scaling require you to define specific instance counts to add/remove. Scheduled is time-based, not metric-based.

questions.question: An EC2 instance passes the EC2 health check but fails the ELB health check. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: The EC2 instance hardware has failed
The instance is in the Pending state
The application inside the instance has crashed or is not responding
The CloudWatch alarm has fired

explanation.correct: EC2 health checks only detect infrastructure issues. ELB checks the application's HTTP response — a failed ELB check with a passing EC2 check means the app is broken but the instance is alive.
explanation.why: Hardware failure would fail both checks. Pending state prevents checks. CloudWatch alarm is unrelated to health check results.

questions.question: What is the purpose of Connection Draining (Deregistration Delay) in a Load Balancer?

options.text: To speed up instance termination
To allow in-flight requests to complete before the instance is removed from the Target Group
To drain the EC2 instance's disk before shutdown
To stop health checks on terminating instances

explanation.correct: Connection Draining stops sending new requests to a terminating instance but allows existing in-flight requests to finish within the configured timeout — preventing broken user sessions.
explanation.why: It doesn't speed up termination. It has nothing to do with disk. Health checks are a separate concept.

questions.question: Your application takes 4 minutes to fully start. What health check grace period should you set?

options.text: 60 seconds
180 seconds
240 seconds or more
The default 300 seconds is always sufficient

explanation.correct: The grace period should be at least 60 seconds longer than your app startup time. If startup takes 4 minutes (240 seconds), set grace period to at least 240 seconds — ideally 300 or more as a buffer.
explanation.why: 60 and 180 seconds are too short for a 4-minute startup. The default of 300 seconds happens to work here but relying on 'default is always fine' is wrong thinking.

questions.question: An ASG has Simple Scaling configured to add 2 instances when CPU > 70%. CPU spikes to 95% and 2 instances are added. CPU remains at 90%. What happens during the cooldown?

options.text: ASG immediately adds 2 more instances because CPU is still high
ASG terminates the 2 new instances
No scaling action occurs until the cooldown period expires
ASG switches to Step Scaling automatically

explanation.correct: Simple Scaling has a cooldown period during which no scaling actions occur. Even if CPU remains high at 90%, ASG waits for the cooldown to expire before evaluating the alarm again.
explanation.why: This is the major limitation of Simple Scaling — it cannot respond rapidly to sustained high load during its own cooldown period.

questions.question: Which termination policy does AWS use by default when an ASG needs to scale in?

options.text: NewestInstance — terminate the most recently launched instance
OldestInstance — terminate the oldest running instance
Default — balance AZs first, then terminate the instance with the oldest launch template
ClosestToNextInstanceHour — terminate based on billing optimization

explanation.correct: The Default Termination Policy first selects the AZ with the most instances (to balance AZs), then terminates the instance using the oldest launch template or configuration version.
explanation.why: NewestInstance and ClosestToNextInstanceHour are valid policies but not the default. OldestInstance is also a valid option but not the default behavior.

questions.question: You have an Application Load Balancer routing amazon.com/orders to Target Group A and amazon.com/cart to Target Group B. What is this called?

options.text: Host-based routing
IP-based routing
Path-based routing
Port-based routing

explanation.correct: Path-based routing routes requests to different Target Groups based on the URL path (e.g., /orders vs /cart). This is a core feature of Application Load Balancers.
explanation.why: Host-based routing uses the domain name (e.g., orders.amazon.com). IP and port-based routing are different concepts.

questions.question: Step Scaling is triggered by a CloudWatch alarm at 70% CPU and adds 2 instances. Immediately after, CPU jumps to 90% (above the next step threshold). What can Step Scaling do that Simple Scaling cannot?

options.text: Step Scaling can still trigger an additional scaling action because it uses warmup, not cooldown
Step Scaling will wait 300 seconds before responding to the 90% alarm
Step Scaling cancels the first scaling action and replaces it
Step Scaling only responds once per alarm state

explanation.correct: Step Scaling uses instance warmup instead of a hard cooldown — it can continue evaluating alarm conditions and potentially add more instances if the load worsens, unlike Simple Scaling which blocks all action during cooldown.
explanation.why: The 300-second block is Simple Scaling's cooldown, not Step Scaling's behavior. Step Scaling doesn't cancel actions; it can stack them.

questions.question: An EC2 instance is in the 'Terminating:Wait' state. What does this indicate?

options.text: The instance failed a health check and is waiting for review
A lifecycle hook is paused, allowing custom cleanup actions before final termination
The instance is waiting for its billing hour to end
ASG is waiting for the grace period to expire

explanation.correct: Terminating:Wait means a lifecycle hook has paused the termination. This gives you time to run cleanup tasks like draining database connections or saving state before the instance is permanently deleted.
explanation.why: Health check failures lead to Terminating, not Terminating:Wait. Billing and grace period are different concepts.

questions.question: Which of the following scenarios is BEST suited for Scheduled Scaling?

options.text: A social media site that gets random viral traffic spikes
A banking app that gets consistently heavy load every weekday from 9 AM to 5 PM
An e-commerce site during an unannounced flash sale
A gaming API with completely unpredictable player counts

explanation.correct: Scheduled Scaling is perfect for predictable, time-based traffic patterns — like office hours banking traffic. You know exactly when load will come, so you schedule the scale-out and scale-in.
explanation.why: Viral spikes, flash sales, and unpredictable loads are better handled by Target Tracking or Step Scaling, which react to actual current conditions.

questions.question: A company wants each microservice (orders, payments, inventory) to scale independently based on its own load. What is the correct ASG + ALB architecture?

options.text: One ASG and one Target Group for all microservices
One ASG per microservice, each with its own Target Group, behind one ALB with path-based routing
Three separate ALBs, one per microservice, each with one ASG
One ASG with multiple Launch Templates, one per microservice

explanation.correct: The microservices pattern uses one ALB with path-based routing to route to multiple Target Groups, each backed by its own ASG. This allows independent scaling per service while keeping one public endpoint.
explanation.why: One ASG for all means they all scale together — not independent. Three ALBs is costly and unnecessary. One ASG cannot manage separate service fleets independently.

questions.question: You're designing a high-traffic news platform. Traffic is normally 1,000 req/sec but spikes to 50,000 req/sec during breaking news events, with no predictable pattern. Which combination of scaling policies would be most effective?

options.text: Simple Scaling + Scheduled Scaling
Target Tracking Scaling + Predictive Scaling
Step Scaling + Scheduled Scaling
Simple Scaling only

explanation.correct: Target Tracking handles the reactive scaling during unpredictable spikes (keeping metrics at target). If the platform has recurring daily news cycles, Predictive Scaling can forecast and pre-provision instances ahead of expected peaks — minimizing the lag in response time.
explanation.why: Simple Scaling has a cooldown problem during rapid spikes. Scheduled doesn't work for unpredictable events. Step Scaling alone doesn't proactively provision.

questions.question: A health check grace period is set to 60 seconds but instances take 5 minutes to start. What is the consequence?

options.text: Health checks are delayed by 5 minutes automatically
New instances are repeatedly terminated and relaunched in a cycle because they fail health checks before they finish starting
ASG disables health checks on new instances permanently
The Load Balancer waits for the instance to respond regardless of grace period

explanation.correct: If the grace period is shorter than startup time, new instances will fail health checks (they're still booting), get marked Unhealthy, terminated, and replaced — only to be terminated again. This creates an infinite replace loop.
explanation.why: Grace period is not auto-adjusted. ASG never disables health checks permanently. The Load Balancer respects the ASG grace period setting.

questions.question: Your Step Scaling policy has three steps. While step 1 is executing (adding 2 instances), another alarm fires triggering step 2. What does Step Scaling do?

options.text: Ignores step 2 because step 1 is still in progress
Cancels step 1 and executes step 2 instead
Evaluates the current metric against all steps and applies the appropriate step adjustment, potentially adding more capacity on top
Waits for the cooldown period before evaluating step 2

explanation.correct: Step Scaling can evaluate additional scaling actions during instance warmup. If the metric has moved into a higher step, ASG can add more capacity proportionally — this is why Step Scaling responds better than Simple Scaling to rapidly worsening conditions.
explanation.why: Step Scaling doesn't ignore additional triggers during warmup. It doesn't cancel in-progress actions. Cooldown is a Simple Scaling concept.

questions.question: You have a Target Group with Connection Draining set to 0 seconds. A user is uploading a 500MB file. ASG terminates the instance mid-upload. What happens?

options.text: The upload is gracefully completed before termination
The upload is immediately interrupted and the connection is dropped
The Load Balancer reroutes the upload to another instance automatically
The instance is protected from termination until the upload completes

explanation.correct: Setting deregistration delay to 0 means the Load Balancer immediately removes the instance with no grace for in-flight requests. The upload is instantly cut off.
explanation.why: With 0 seconds delay, there is no graceful completion. Load Balancers cannot migrate active TCP connections mid-stream. Instance Protection is a separate feature (and not about uploads).

questions.question: An ASG has min=2, desired=4, max=8. Step Scaling tries to add 6 instances (to reach 10 total). What actually happens?

options.text: ASG adds all 6 instances and temporarily goes above max
ASG only adds 4 instances, capping at the max of 8
ASG rejects the scaling action entirely because it exceeds max
ASG terminates 2 instances first, then adds 6

explanation.correct: ASG always respects the maximum capacity. If current count is 4 and the policy wants to add 6 (total 10), ASG will only add 4 instances — reaching the max of 8. It never exceeds the maximum.
explanation.why: Going above max is never allowed. The action isn't rejected — it's simply capped. ASG doesn't terminate instances to make room for more in this scenario.

questions.question: Which statement about ELB health checks and ASG is TRUE?

options.text: Enabling ELB health checks replaces EC2 health checks
Both EC2 and ELB health checks run simultaneously — if either fails, the instance is replaced
ELB health checks only apply to the Load Balancer, not the ASG
ELB health checks are mandatory for all ASGs

explanation.correct: Both health check types run simultaneously. The ASG description in the console states: 'all are evaluated, and if at least one fails, instance replacement occurs.' EC2 checks are always on; ELB checks are additive.
explanation.why: ELB checks don't replace EC2 checks. Both apply to the ASG. ELB health checks are optional (recommended, not mandatory).

questions.question: What happens to instances in the 'Pending' state regarding health checks?

options.text: Health checks run immediately on Pending instances
Pending instances are protected from health checks during the grace period
Pending instances are always marked Healthy
ASG pauses all health checks whenever any instance is Pending

explanation.correct: Instances in the Pending state (being launched) are protected from health check evaluation for the duration of the health check grace period, preventing premature termination during startup.
explanation.why: Health checks don't run immediately on Pending instances. They're not auto-marked Healthy. ASG doesn't pause all checks globally just because one instance is Pending.

questions.question: You need an ALB to route requests differently based on the domain name (orders.company.com vs payments.company.com). Which routing feature do you use?

options.text: Path-based routing
Host-based routing
IP-based routing
Weight-based routing

explanation.correct: Host-based routing routes requests based on the Host header (domain name) in the HTTP request. Different subdomains can route to different Target Groups using a single ALB.
explanation.why: Path-based routing uses the URL path (/orders, /payments). IP-based routing targets specific IP addresses. Weight-based is for canary deployments.

questions.question: What is the maximum configurable deregistration delay (Connection Draining timeout) on an ALB Target Group?

options.text: 300 seconds
600 seconds
1800 seconds
3600 seconds

explanation.correct: The deregistration delay can be configured from 0 to 3600 seconds (1 hour). The default is 300 seconds. For long-running operations, you might increase it significantly.
explanation.why: 300 is the default, not the maximum. 600 and 1800 are valid values within the range but not the maximum.

questions.question: A company runs a Lambda function that processes images and stores results in S3. They want to add Auto Scaling-style behavior. Which statement is TRUE?

options.text: You must use EC2 Auto Scaling Groups with Lambda
Lambda scales automatically — you don't need ASG
Lambda uses Step Scaling internally
Lambda requires CloudWatch alarms to scale

explanation.correct: AWS Lambda scales automatically and concurrently without needing an Auto Scaling Group. Each invocation can run in parallel up to the account's concurrency limit. ASG is specifically for EC2-based workloads.
explanation.why: Lambda doesn't use ASG, Step Scaling internally, or require CloudWatch alarms to scale — it responds to invocations directly.
